## Where the Framing Breaks Down

Treating the X-8 through the keystone of transparent carriage is productive and it misleads in at least five ways.

**The X-8 is not one vehicle.** The designation covers five sub-variants, four of them flown, with two different engines, two pressurisation schemes, and in two cases no booster at all, as [Parsch][ref_parsch_aerobee_hi] lists them. Statements about the performance of the X-8 are therefore statements about a specific sub-variant, and the published summary figures blend them.

**The X-designation covers only the Air Force slice.** The identical airframe flown by the Navy the same month was an RTV-N-10 and by the Army Signal Corps an XASR-SC-2, as the version table in [Aerobee][ref_aerobee] shows, and neither is an X-plane. An article organised around the X-number is therefore organised around a procurement boundary rather than around an engineering object, and it inherits that boundary's arbitrariness. The [list of X-planes][ref_list_of_xplanes] records the X-8 without remarking on it.

**The vehicle was sometimes the experiment after all.** The Aerobee 150 pitch-coupling investigation of [Busse and Kraft 1966][research_busse_1966_2], the Aerobee 350 flight-dynamics work of [Lawrence 1965][research_lawrence_1965], and the propulsion-failure analysis of [Bushnell and Busse 1967][research_bushnell_1967] are all cases where the vehicle's own behaviour was the object of study. The transparency framing does not describe them.

**The vehicle is not the achievement.** Almost everything in the What the Data Changed section was the work of the payload groups at the Naval Research Laboratory, the Applied Physics Laboratory, the Air Force Cambridge Research Center, American Science and Engineering, and a dozen universities. Organising a history around the carrier systematically under-credits the people who built the instruments, and the Nobel Prize that came out of an Aerobee flight went to the instrument builders rather than to Aerojet, correctly.

**Calling it spin-stabilised is wrong**, although [Mattson and Tagg 1995][ref_mattson_tagg_1995] and [Aerojet General X-8][ref_aerojet_x8] both do. The X-8 is aerodynamically stabilised by fins, as [Aerobee][ref_aerobee] describes it, and rolls slowly to average out asymmetries. A spin-stabilised vehicle is stabilised gyroscopically and requires no aerodynamic restoring moment at all, a different mechanism with different failure modes. The distinction matters because the roll-resonance hazard analysed above exists **only** for the fin-stabilised case, since a genuinely spin-stabilised body has no pitch natural frequency to resonate with.

## The Source Base

The archival situation for this vehicle is the reverse of the [X-6][related_post_a303_convair_x6], and the contrast is instructive enough to record.

The X-6's record lives in the Department of Energy's technical archive because its subject was a reactor, and a standard aerospace search returns almost nothing. A search of that same archive, the [Office of Scientific and Technical Information][ref_osti], abbreviated OSTI, for the Aerobee and its designations returns nothing relevant at all.

The X-8's record is spread across two archives rather than one, and the second changes the picture materially.

The NASA Technical Reports Server, abbreviated NTRS, is rich from about 1959 onward and thin before it, because it accessioned NASA-era material comprehensively and the earlier Navy and Air Force material only sporadically. A search of [NTRS][ref_ntrs] for this subject returns several times as many reports from the 1960s as from the 1950s. **On that evidence alone the X-8 era would appear poorly documented, and that appearance is misleading.**

Reports held by the Defense Technical Information Center are registered with Crossref under a single publisher prefix, so they resolve by digital object identifier like any journal article and verify the same way. Its holdings on this subject reach back to the 1940s. They include the research and development report on the Navy Aerobee-Hi, the Naval Research Laboratory Upper Atmosphere Research Report series, wind-variability studies underpinning impact prediction, roll-resonance analysis, and per-round meteorological data reports naming individual Aerobee vehicles. Every identifier cited in the article's prose, from either archive or from the journal literature, has been resolved and compared on title through [Crossref][ref_crossref], and every identifier in the survey is the archive's own, taken from the record it names. **The material that the aerospace archive lacks for the 1946 to 1958 period is largely in the defence archive**, so the thinness of the early record belongs to one archive rather than to the period.

The bias that remains is narrower than the aerospace archive alone suggests, but it is real. **The Aerobee 150 and 350 are still better documented than the X-8 itself**, because the later vehicles were flown under an agency that published, and the Applied Physics Laboratory material of the earliest years survives mainly through the report series and through journal publication.

Three consequences follow for this article. Vehicle parameters are drawn from secondary compilations rather than from primary specifications, and where those compilations disagree the disagreement is reported. Flight-by-flight detail for the X-8 proper rests on a narrower base than the analysis built on it, and the counts in the flight-test section are the visible symptom of that. The science results are the best-documented part of the whole subject, because they were published in the open literature at the time, which is why What the Data Changed cites 97 research works, more than any section except The Contemporary Literature.

**The survey rests on 7,715 research records drawn from Crossref, the NASA Technical Reports Server and the Defense Technical Information Center**, of which 1,489 are report primaries by the identifier rule set out under The Definition of Primary, being 19.3 percent. Of the 7,568 dated records, the median year of publication is 1997, 362 were published before 1960, and 2,255, or 29.9 percent, in 2015 or later. The article's own argument rests on the 363 research records cited in its prose before this section, of which 154 are report primaries.

### The Definition of Primary

**Primacy is a property of the document, and this survey derives it from the identifier.** A record is a report primary when it is a NASA Technical Reports Server record or carries a digital object identifier under the 10.21236 prefix, which Crossref registers for Defense Technical Information Center reports. By that rule 918 records are NASA Technical Reports Server records and 571 are Defense Technical Information Center reports.

**The rule undercounts what is first-hand for this vehicle more than for most.** The first results of the rocket programme were published by the experimenters themselves in Physical Review, Nature and the Journal of Geophysical Research, so the papers that report what the Aerobee measured are journal articles and an identifier rule counts them as secondary. 19.3 percent is a lower bound on how much of this survey is first-hand.

### Thin Subjects

**Five subjects that this article's derivations depend on have thin literatures.** Each count below is the number of research records in this survey whose title carries at least one of the listed terms, with a hyphen read as a space and a term matching where a word begins with it.

| Subject | Title terms counted | Records |
|---|---|---|
| the observing time above a threshold altitude and the number of flights a measurement needs | observing time, observation time, time above, exposure time, number of flights, sample size, statistical power | 0 |
| wind weighting and launcher setting for unguided rockets | wind weighting, wind compensation, ballistic wind, launcher setting | 10 |
| deliberate tumbling and fin ejection before parachute recovery | tumbl, fin ejection, fin separation, fin release | 0 |
| aspect determination from two vector references | aspect sensor, aspect determination, aspect camera, aspect solution, two vector, triad, wahba, sun sensor and magnetometer, magnetometer and sun sensor | 12 |
| the pressurant mass of a pressure-fed stage and the choice of helium over air | pressurant mass, pressurant requirement, pressurant gas requirement, helium mass, helium quantity, pressurant consumption | 6 |

**The keystone relation of this article is not a subject of the literature at all.** No record carries any of the observing-time or sample-size terms, which is consistent with a result that follows from the flight time of a projectile and the two-sample power calculation and is therefore stated in textbooks rather than in papers, so the article's claim stands on the arithmetic.

**Wind weighting is a small and old literature.** Nine of its ten records were published between 1967 and 1985, which is the signature of a technique worked out for unguided rockets and then made unnecessary for most vehicles by guidance.

**The fin ejection that turns a falling body into a tumbling one has no literature of its own in this survey.** No record carries the terms counted, and the reduction in opening load that justifies the technique is derived in this article from the ballistic coefficient rather than taken from a source.

**Aspect determination from two reference vectors is a satellite literature.** Its twelve records are dominated by spacecraft attitude estimation from sun sensors and magnetometers, the same two-cone geometry the Aerobee aspect system solved, and one of them concerns a sounding rocket.

**The pressurant literature is about cryogens.** Five of the six records on pressurant mass concern cryogenic or liquid-hydrogen tanks, so the storable pressure-fed case and the choice of helium over air that this article computes are not treated in their own right.

### What the Survey Admits

**The research survey admits a record only when a person reading its title finds it on this article's subject.** Candidate records are drawn from Crossref, the NASA Technical Reports Server and the Defense Technical Information Center by title against this article's subject vocabulary, which names the sounding rocket and its family, its propellants, engine, motors, tanks and structure, the flight mechanics of an unguided finned rocket, recovery, telemetry, attitude and the payload environment, range safety and launch cost, and the upper-atmosphere, solar and astronomical science the vehicle carried, and every report that the two report servers return for this subject's own queries is proposed as well. Every title so drawn has then been read, so the vocabulary proposes records and the reading decides them. Four filters kept for other articles are switched off here because their families are part of this subject, namely missile aerodynamics, hypersonic heating, meteorology and physiology.

**Many words this subject depends on also name something else, and a record that shares only such a word is excluded.** Rocket also names a salad plant, a stove, a clinical trial of an anticoagulant and the idiom of difficulty. Sounding also names the echo sounding of the sea floor and the electrical sounding of the ground. Recovery also names economic, medical and industrial recovery, and the parachute also names the seed of a dandelion, the severance of an executive and the parachutist. The launch tower is not a cooling tower or a wind-turbine tower, and the launcher of a multiple-rocket weapon system is studied for its fire control rather than its flight mechanics. Telemetry also names medical monitoring, and pulse-position modulation also names optical and ultra-wideband communication. Ozone also names water treatment and urban air quality, Lyman-alpha also names the absorbers of cosmology and a hygrometer, and X-ray also names diffraction and radiography. The nozzle of a sprayer, a printer or a diesel injector is not a rocket nozzle, the roll of a ship or a rolling mill is not the roll of a rocket, and the spin of an electron is not the spin of a vehicle. Boil-off also names the gas of liquefied natural gas carriers, the falling sphere also names a viscometer, the grenade also names a weapon and a dictionary headword, and anomalous sound propagation also names acoustics in solids and in the sea. Correction, erratum, retraction and withdrawal notices, unsigned news items and new-book notices, supplementary material, and the indexes, bibliographies, front matter and appendix tables of books are excluded as well, because a survey counts research works and those are editorial events or parts of works. A review of a book or a referee's comment on a manuscript, a reference or definition entry of two pages or fewer and a second deposit of a document already in the survey, such as an archive copy, a preprint, a meeting abstract or an abstract-journal listing of it, are not admitted either, while an authored encyclopedia article of more than two pages and a textbook chapter are research works and are kept. A deposit whose folded title is that of a record read as off topic is excluded with it.

**Some records of doubtful relevance are kept.** Spin-stabilised gun projectiles share their roll, coning and Magnus aerodynamics with the finned rocket. Attitude determination of small satellites from sun sensors and magnetometers is the two-vector problem the Aerobee aspect system solved. The buckling of axially compressed cylindrical shells in general is the knockdown problem behind tanks as structure, and the corrosion and analysis of fuming nitric acid is the handling problem of the propellant. Satellite drag measurements of thermospheric density, cosmic rays measured at high altitude, orbital ultraviolet observation of the sun and reviews of the cosmic X-ray background continue measurements that began on rockets, and so do ionospheric studies by ground radio and satellite methods. Each is kept for what it shares with this subject, and a reader may weigh it accordingly.

**Every research title has been read for relevance**, so the off-topic share that remains is a matter of reading judgement, and no sample measures it.

## Epistemic State

**Historical fact, well documented.** The Aerobee originated in a 1946 Navy contract to Aerojet instigated by Van Allen at the Applied Physics Laboratory. The name is a contraction of Aerojet and Bumblebee. The first dummy flight was 25 September 1947 and the first fully successful flight 5 March 1948. The first Air Force flight was USAF-1 from Holloman on 2 December 1949, reaching 96.0 kilometres, and its nose cone was lost until July 1950 with the film destroyed. The Aerobee family flew 1,037 times, ending on 17 January 1985. The Scorpius X-1 detection was made from an Aerobee 150 on 19 June 1962 and reported by Giacconi and colleagues.

**Engineering analysis, computed here.** The optical-depth altitudes of 80 and 110 kilometres, the observing-time relation and its 400 second coefficient, the theoretical specific impulse of 224 seconds, the nozzle throat and exit dimensions recovered from the thrust difference, the exit Mach number of 2.76 and the thrust coefficients of 1.624 in vacuum and 1.409 at sea level, the chamber pressure of 2.16 megapascals recovered jointly with those coefficients, the measured characteristic velocity of 1,393 metres per second against an ideal 1,505 and the resulting 93 percent combustion efficiency, the throat heat flux of 9.3 megawatts per square metre, the booster web and burning area, the cryogenic boil-off rate of 18 percent per hour, the tank mass fraction, the helium against air pressurant comparison, the net axial tension that keeps the shell out of compression, the radiation equilibrium wall temperature of 943 kelvin, the tower exit velocity of 99 metres per second, the pitch natural frequency of 1.16 radians per second, the damping ratio of 0.0033 and the 0.86 second divergence time constant, the fin normal-force slope, the seven kilometre wind displacement, the two-dimensional containment radii, the 62 degree coning half-angle, the turbopause density criterion, the photon-counting exposure of 150 seconds, the roll-resonance density scaling and its critical densities, the tumbling ballistic-coefficient reduction of a factor of 63, the parachute sizing and opening load, the telemetry link budget and the photographic comparison, the buckling and thermal calculations, and the drag-loss estimate are all derived in this article from the stated inputs. **Each depends on assumed values that are named where they are used**, and a reader substituting different assumptions will get different numbers.

**Inference, stated as such.** That the propellant was chosen for operational tempo over performance is inferred from the trade and is not a documented decision. That the fins were jettisoned specifically to reduce parachute opening load is an inference from the physics, since the sources record the practice without stating the reason. That the X-8 designation reflects administrative convenience rather than a decision to broaden the X-series is an inference from the absence of any recorded decision.

**An independent check.** Carrying the recovered chamber pressure back to vacuum reproduces the separately reported thrust of 4,728 pounds to within one pound.

**The X-8 designation dates from 1951.** [Parsch][ref_parsch_pre1963] dates the redesignation of RTV-A-1 to X-8 to May 1951, when the Air Force gave its missiles aircraft designations, and [Parsch][ref_parsch_aerobee_hi] gives 1951 for the RTV-A-1 and all four of its lettered variants. The Air Force's statistical digests support the year without naming the Aerobee. The [digest for fiscal year 1951][ref_usaf_digest_fy1951] lists the Shrike as RTV-A-4 in the same table that lists the Rascal as B-63, and the [digest for fiscal year 1952][ref_usaf_digest_fy1952], covering the year to 30 June 1952, lists the Shrike as X-9. Because the digests omit the Aerobee, they date the move of the research test vehicles in general, and the X-8 date rests on Parsch's account that the series moved together. Every dated reading falls after the first Air Force flight of 2 December 1949, seventeen months after it on Parsch's date and at most thirty months after it on the digests. The year 1949 that the [list of X-planes][ref_list_of_xplanes] gives against the X-8 is a first-flight year, since that list dates each entry by first flight or cancellation. No source consulted supports a redesignation in 1955. When the Air Force dropped aircraft designations for missiles on 15 August 1955, [Parsch][ref_parsch_pre1963] records that existing X-type research vehicles kept their designations. Usage lagged the change. Aerojet's report for May 1954 [Walker 1954][research_walker_1954] still names a Modified Model RTV-A-1a, and [Mattson and Tagg 1995][ref_mattson_tagg_1995] write that the Air Force vehicles were ordered under the X-8 designator, a phrasing written in 1995 that gives no date and that the order as RTV-A-1 recorded by [Aerojet General X-8][ref_aerojet_x8] contradicts. A primary nomenclature record naming the X-8 itself was not located.

**Not settled by the record consulted here.**

The relationship between X-8 and RM-84. [Aerojet General X-8][ref_aerojet_x8] states the vehicle was renamed RM-84 after being X-8, citing Parsch, but [Parsch][ref_parsch_pre1963] applies XRM-84 only to a variant of the Aerobee-Hi, which is a different vehicle. Both cannot be right as stated.

The flown and delivered counts. Sixty X-8 flights are reported in one place, with a breakdown that sums to sixty, and deliveries of 66 vehicles in another, with a launch table giving 61. The distinction between delivered and flown accounts for part of it and is not stated by any source consulted.

The last X-8A flight date, given as 11/12/1956 in a source using an ambiguous numeric format, which is either 12 November or 11 December 1956. The launch table's 12 November 1956 for the RTV-A-1a is consistent with the first reading.

The launch tower height. [Mattson and Tagg 1995][ref_mattson_tagg_1995] report the normal X-8 tower at Holloman as 143 feet, which is 43.6 metres, and give 142 and 152 feet for the same tower at other dates and nearly 60 feet for the first launch, [Fraser 1985][ref_fraser_1985] gives 140 feet with 90 feet of guided travel for the Applied Physics Laboratory tower at White Sands, and [Wade][ref_astronautix_aerobee] gives 53 metres for Aerobee towers generally. The tower-exit calculation in this article uses the full 43.6 metres, would give 110 metres per second at 53, and would give less over a shorter guided length.

The burnout figures. The burnout velocity of 4,420 feet per second at 17 nautical miles rests on [White 2011][ref_white_2011_x8] alone, which matches the speed [Parsch][ref_parsch_aerobee_hi] gives for the original Aerobee, while [Mattson and Tagg 1995][ref_mattson_tagg_1995] give a maximum velocity of 3,600 miles per hour about 33 seconds after launch.

The internal consistency of the published performance figures. The staged reconstruction at the 40 second sustainer burn falls 209 metres per second short of the reported burnout velocity before any drag is counted, against an independent drag-loss estimate of 60 to 150. One or more of the booster inert mass, the sustainer burn time, and the specific impulse is therefore off, a burn between 47 and 49 seconds would close the figures on its own, and the record does not say which.

Whether the reported five percent design conservatism reflects physical margin or numerical error in the hand integration. The Euler truncation error of a one-second step is 3.8 percent, which is the same size, and the two cannot be separated from the public record.

Whether any payload fragments from the 16 October 1957 Aerobee shaped-charge experiment reached escape velocity. Zwicky claimed at the time that at least two did. A later analysis by McDowell concludes that none did. **This article takes no position** and notes only that the claim was contemporaneously compared to Sputnik in the press.

## Out of Scope

The Aerobee-Hi, the Aerobee 100, 150, 170, 300, and 350, and the Nike-boosted derivatives are treated here only where they illuminate the X-8. They are the larger part of the family's history and they carry no X-designation.

The V-2 programme, Project Hermes, and the Bumper firings are the X-8's context rather than its subject. The Viking and Vanguard vehicles, which were the Naval Research Laboratory's competing line, are mentioned only for contrast.

The science results are surveyed rather than assessed. The X-ray astronomy that began on an Aerobee has a fifty-year literature of its own, and the ionospheric and aeronomic results likewise. Nothing here evaluates whether any particular result stood up.

The designation-system question raised in the opening is stated rather than resolved, because resolving it requires the later cases. It returns in the closing article of this series.

Sounding rockets of other nations, including the British Skylark, the Japanese Kappa series, and the Soviet vertical-probe rockets, are outside the X-designation entirely and are not covered.

## Conclusion

The X-8 is the first vehicle in this series that was not built to be studied. It was built to carry, and everything unusual about it follows from that.

Optical depth set the requirement, and observing time was the figure of merit. Both are logarithmic in the quantity a programme pays for, which is mass ratio, and the consequence is that a sounding-rocket programme buys precision by flying often rather than by flying high. The vehicle was therefore optimised for cheapness and repeatability at every point where those competed with performance. It burned a mediocre storable propellant so it could sit on the tower. It used pressurised tanks so it needed no turbopump. It made the tanks the structure so it needed no airframe. It had no guidance, so it needed a tower and a desert. It rolled to average out its own manufacturing errors, and accepted a resonance hazard in exchange. It threw its fins away so the parachute would survive, and it recovered its nose cone physically because the information in a photographic plate exceeded the entire telemetry capacity of the flight by a factor of about twenty-five.

**None of these are good engineering in the abstract and all of them are correct for the use.** The X-7 carried the same lesson in a different currency.

What it produced is out of proportion to what it was. The first vertical ozone profile, the first measured atmosphere above 30 kilometres, the first far-ultraviolet solar spectra, the first solar X-ray flare observation, the first neutral composition by mass spectrometry, and the discovery of the first X-ray source outside the solar system all came from the sounding-rocket programme to which this vehicle belonged, the earliest of them from the captured V-2 rockets that the Aerobee replaced. One of them earned a Nobel Prize. **The observation lasted a few minutes**, and the reason a few minutes sufficed is the relation this article opens with.

The designation is the loose end. The X-8 is an X-plane by administrative act rather than by any property it possesses. It is the first case where the letter stopped meaning experimental aircraft and started meaning experimental vehicle. Nobody appears to have decided that. It became true, and the rest of this series is in part the story of how far it went.
